titleEn: In Your strength the king rejoices
progression: | Em Em | Am Am | Em B7 | Em Em |
intro: Fourteen verses, a royal psalm, commonly read as the companion to Psalm 20: there the king goes out and the people pray for him, here he comes back and the psalm counts what he was given. The grammar to watch is the ending -kha, Your, glued onto noun after noun: Your strength, Your salvation, Your hand, Your right hand, Your might. Running against it is the ending -o, his, on everything that belongs to the king: his heart, his head, his glory. Two possessive suffixes arguing about who owns the victory, for thirteen verses, until the last one switches to we.

stichs.en: For the choirmaster.
A psalm of David.

verses.summary: The heading files the psalm under the temple musician before a word of content arrives. Genre and author come after the performance instruction, not before it.

stichs.en: O LORD, the king rejoices in Your strength,
and in Your rescue how greatly he exults!

verses.summary: The first thing said about the king is that he is glad, and both halves of the gladness sit inside a noun carrying Your. He owns the joy, God owns the strength.

stichs.en: You have given him the desire of his heart,
and the request of his lips You have not withheld.
Selah.

verses.summary: Past tense throughout. This is a receipt rather than a request, and Selah closes the accounting before the reasons begin.

stichs.en: For You meet him with blessings of good,
You set a crown of fine gold on his head.

verses.summary: The first of five verses opening with ki, for. The reasons start here, and the first reason is that the blessing arrived ahead of the asking.

stichs.en: He asked You for life; You gave it to him,
length of days, for ever and ever.

verses.summary: He asked for life. What came back was longer than the question, and the psalm lets the mismatch stand without explaining it.

stichs.en: Great is his glory through Your rescue,
splendour and majesty You place upon him.

verses.summary: The glory is his, but the preposition puts its source outside him. Two abstract nouns are laid on him the way the crown was laid on him in the verse before.

stichs.en: For You make him blessings for ever,
You gladden him with joy at Your presence.

verses.summary: The second ki. Blessing is made permanent, and the joy is located not inside the king but at a face that is not his.

stichs.en: For the king trusts in the LORD,
and through the kindness of the Most High he will not be shaken.

verses.summary: The hinge of the psalm. Everything up to here was gift; this verse names the single thing the king does, trust, and the negative that follows is the whole promise.

stichs.en: Your hand will reach all Your enemies,
Your right hand will reach those who hate You.

verses.summary: The addressee slips here. From this verse to verse 13 the you being spoken to may be God or the king, and the Hebrew never settles it.

stichs.en: You will set them like a furnace of fire at the time of Your presence;
the LORD will swallow them in His anger,
and fire will devour them.

verses.summary: The verb that set a crown on a head in verse 4 now sets enemies alight. Same root, opposite work, and it returns once more in verse 13.

stichs.en: Their fruit You will destroy from the earth,
and their seed from among the children of men.

verses.summary: The threat reaches past the enemy to his descendants, which is the ancient formula for ending a dynasty rather than a life.

stichs.en: For they aimed evil against You,
they devised a scheme, and they will not prevail.

verses.summary: The reason for the violence, given late. The verse grants them the intention and denies them the outcome in the same breath.

stichs.en: For You will make them turn their backs,
with Your bowstrings You will take aim at their faces.

verses.summary: The last picture is archery. The enemy is turned around and the string is drawn at his face, the mirror of the face the king was gladdened by in verse 7.

stichs.en: Be exalted, O LORD, in Your strength;
we will sing and make music of Your might.

glosses: and we will make music of
verses.summary: The only verse in the plural. Thirteen verses about one man end with a congregation singing, which is what keeps the psalm sayable after the king is gone.

pardes.body: Two halves and a frame. Verses 2 to 8 are a report made to God about the king: what he asked for, what he was given, why he will not be shaken. Verses 9 to 13 are a threat against enemies. Verse 14 turns the whole thing into a congregational song, the only place in the psalm where anyone says we. Read verse 5 slowly, because it carries the argument: the king asked for life and was given length of days for ever and ever, which is more than was asked, and the gap between request and gift is what the first half is about.

From verse 9 the pronouns go slippery. {{9.1}}, Your hand, can belong to God, who has been the You of the whole psalm, or to the king, who has been the him. The 1917 English in the source file hesitates in exactly this way: inside verse 9 it writes Thy hand with a capital and those that hate thee with a small letter, then drops to lowercase for the rest. The Hebrew marks nothing. Watch the noun for face as well: at {{7.7}} it is joy at Your presence, at {{10.4}} it is the time of Your face, and the same word carries the reward and the burning. The verb of setting behaves the same way, placing a crown at {{4.4}} and setting enemies alight at {{10.0}}.

Read as prophecy rather than court poetry, the king here is the messianic king, and verse 5 stops being flattery: life asked for, length of days for ever and ever granted, becomes a statement about the world to come rather than a long reign. The crown of {{4.6}} and {{4.7}}, fine gold set on the head before any battle is mentioned, is read the same way, as the end of the story placed at the beginning. This is a reading and not the plain sense, and it is worth holding the two apart: the plain sense of verse 4 is a coronation, with a real crown and a real head.

The abstract nouns of this psalm are, in kabbalistic vocabulary, names of the sefirot, and they arrive in a run: kindness at {{8.4}}, splendour at {{6.3}} and majesty at {{6.4}}, strength at {{14.2}} and might at {{14.5}}. Read that way the psalm is not listing a king's assets but naming the channels through which he receives, and the closing verb, we will sing, is what a receiver does once the channel is open. The crown of verse 4 is set on the head from outside rather than grown from within, which in this vocabulary is the mark of a light that surrounds and is never contained.
